vi-peel.summary: A branded medium-depth peel that resurfaces skin for clearer, more even tone and smoother texture across skin tones.

quick.overview:
The VI Peel is a branded medium-depth chemical peel from the Vitality Institute, marketed for acne, pigment, sun damage, scars and fine lines. The payoff people want is clearer, more even, smoother skin.

The blend combines trichloroacetic acid, phenol, salicylic acid, tretinoin and vitamin C to exfoliate the epidermis and upper dermis, after which skin sheds and renews. Published research is a few small studies, including a 2024 study of 30 patients who had a peel and a neurotoxin treatment on the same day. Exact ingredient ratios are proprietary.
quick.how: It is applied by a clinician as an in-office treatment, and the skin peels over the following days. People often pair it with a neurotoxin visit, as in the 30-patient study, and with sunscreen and gentle skincare afterward. Marketing says it suits all skin tones.
quick.risks: Peel side effects include redness, peeling and pigment change. Because it is a medium-depth peel containing phenol and tretinoin, healing takes longer than with a light peel, and product-specific safety data are sparse. People who are pregnant or prone to pigment changes should raise this with the clinician.

angle.text: People use the VI Peel to clear acne marks, fade pigment and sun damage, and smooth fine lines. The multi-acid blend peels away damaged outer skin and the skin renews, leaving a clearer, more even surface. It is marketed for all skin tones, and published data are a few small studies.

obagi-blue-peel.summary: A branded, standardized TCA peel that goes deeper than light peels to smooth and even out skin.

quick.overview:
The Obagi Blue Peel is a branded TCA-based medium peel used to smooth texture and even out skin tone. It is designed to reach deeper than superficial exfoliating peels.

TCA causes a controlled injury to the epidermis and upper dermis, after which the skin sheds and renews, and collagen remodels. A 1999 paper described it as a standardized method with depth control. Other published work includes a 2002 comparison with an Er:YAG laser for photoaged hands and a 2006 paper on performing the peel faster and more cheaply.
quick.how: A clinician applies it in the office, and skin flakes and peels over the following days to a week or so. People usually follow it with strict sun protection and gentle care while the skin heals.
quick.risks: Medium peels carry risks of pigment change, prolonged redness and scarring. Results depend on technique and patient selection, and it should be performed by a trained clinician.

angle.text: People use the Blue Peel for smoother, more even skin than a light peel gives. The TCA creates a controlled injury of predictable depth, the skin renews and collagen remodels. A 1999 paper described the standardized method, and published studies are few.

pca-peel.summary: A line of professional acid peels that refresh skin for a brighter, more even complexion.

quick.overview:
PCA Peel is a line of professional chemical peels from PCA Skin, used for general skin renewal and pigment concerns. People book it for fresher, more even-looking skin.

The signature peel is described by the company as a modified Jessner's formula (lactic, salicylic, kojic and citric acids with resorcinol), with TCA and lactic acid blends in the wider range. The acids exfoliate the skin surface, and the skin sheds and renews. The company reports its own clinical testing, and no independent published trials of the PCA Peel were found.
quick.how: It is applied in a clinic or esthetician's treatment room, often as a series of sessions. The brand describes its peel as self-neutralizing, and users commonly combine it with home skincare and sunscreen.
quick.risks: Peels can cause irritation, burning, redness and peeling; consumer reviews cited in one source mention these. Pigment change is a general peel risk, and sun protection matters afterward.

angle.text: People use PCA Peels to freshen dull skin and even out pigment. Acid blends loosen the outer skin, which sheds and renews, revealing a brighter, more even surface. Claims come from the manufacturer, and no independent published trials were found.

cosmelan-peel.summary: A depigmenting mask-and-cream protocol from mesoestetic used to fade melasma, dark marks and sun spots for a more even tone.

quick.overview:
Cosmelan is a professional depigmenting treatment from the Spanish company mesoestetic, marketed for melasma, post-inflammatory marks, sun spots and freckles. People use it to fade dark patches and even out skin tone.

It has two phases: a mask applied in clinic and left on for several hours, then roughly six months of home cream and sun protection. The company says it corrects existing spots and regulates melanin production, and that it suits all skin types. These are manufacturer claims, and no peer-reviewed trials were found.
quick.how: The mask goes on in a clinic visit, then a home cream is used daily for months alongside strict sunscreen. Redness and peeling in the first days are typical, and fading builds across the home-care phase.
quick.risks: The company discusses irritation and rebound pigmentation, and stresses sun protection to avoid it. Contraindications listed by the maker include pregnancy, isotretinoin use and a history of vitiligo.

angle.text: People use Cosmelan to fade melasma and dark spots into a more even tone. The mask and months of home cream aim to reduce melanin production so patches lighten. Claims come from the manufacturer, and no published trials were found.

dermamelan.summary: A professional non-hydroquinone depigmenting treatment used to fade melasma and even out skin tone.

quick.overview:
Dermamelan is a professional depigmenting treatment marketed for melasma and uneven pigmentation. People in appearance communities discuss it as a way to even out skin tone and fade dark patches.

It is described in the literature as a non-hydroquinone bleaching formulation, and it is a professional aesthetic treatment rather than a classical chemical peel. It aims to reduce melanin deposits in the skin. A 2011 pilot study used reflectance confocal microscopy to assess its efficacy and safety for melasma, and no larger trials were identified.
quick.how: It is applied by a professional and is usually followed by a home-care routine with sun protection. Pigment lightening develops over weeks to months.
quick.risks: Depigmenting treatments can cause irritation, and dermatology guidance generally calls for professional supervision. The 2011 pilot assessed safety, but larger trials are lacking, so the full side-effect profile is not documented.

angle.text: People use Dermamelan to fade melasma and even out skin tone. It is a non-hydroquinone formula intended to reduce pigment production so dark patches lighten. Support comes from a single small 2011 pilot study.

retinol-peel-retinoic-acid-peel.summary: A clinic-applied tretinoin peel used to smooth photoaged skin and fade pigment.

quick.overview:
A retinoic acid peel applies a tretinoin solution in a clinic to treat photoaging, wrinkles, scars and pigment such as melasma. People use it for smoother, more even skin.

Tretinoin is a retinoid used topically for acne, melasma, scars and aging. As a peel it is applied in a higher concentration, often 5% in studies, to exfoliate the skin and stimulate renewal. Research includes a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial in facial photoaging and comparative trials in acanthosis nigricans. A review notes the field lacks a consensus protocol.
quick.how: A clinician applies it, and it is later washed off or left to act depending on the protocol. It is often preceded by a Jessner's peel and done as a short series. Peeling and flaking follow for several days.
quick.risks: Reported risks include stinging, redness, dryness and pigment changes, rising with depth. Retinoids are generally avoided in pregnancy, and sun protection is important afterward.

angle.text: People use retinoic acid peels to smooth photoaged skin, soften scars and wrinkles, and fade pigment. The retinoid renews skin and stimulates collagen. Trials have studied it in facial photoaging and acanthosis nigricans.

salicylic-acid-peel.summary: The oil-soluble BHA peel most often used for acne and pigment, clearing pores for clearer skin.

quick.overview:
A salicylic acid peel is the superficial peel most often used for acne and some pigmentation. People use it for clearer pores, fewer breakouts and fewer marks.

Salicylic acid is a beta-hydroxy acid described as antibacterial, anti-inflammatory and oil-soluble, which is why it is associated with acne-prone skin. Studies commonly use 20 to 30% concentrations. Published work is mostly small comparative studies and registered trials, such as a 2014 study comparing pyruvic and salicylic peels on sebum secretion in 20 people with acne.
quick.how: A clinician applies it in the office, and it is often repeated as a series of sessions spaced weeks apart. Mild flaking is typical, and people usually keep up sunscreen and acne skincare alongside it.
quick.risks: Light peels commonly cause stinging, redness, irritation and dryness. Deeper peels carry higher complication risks such as pigment change.

angle.text: People use salicylic acid peels to clear acne and reduce the marks it leaves. The oil-soluble acid works into pores, easing breakouts and inflammation so skin looks clearer. Small comparative studies cover its acne use.

glycolic-acid-peel.summary: The most widely studied AHA peel, used for brighter, smoother skin, dark marks, acne scars and fine lines.

quick.overview:
A glycolic acid peel exfoliates the skin with an alpha-hydroxy acid and is used for pigmentation, dark under-eyes, acne scars and fine lines. People use it for brighter, smoother, more even skin.

It loosens dead outer skin cells, which shed and are replaced faster. It has the largest body of studies among the common peels. Studies in Indian and other patient groups have tested concentrations such as 20% and 30% for melasma, periorbital melanosis and acne scars, alone or combined with other agents, though many are small single-center studies.
quick.how: A clinician applies it, usually as a series of sessions a few weeks apart. Skin may look flushed and flake lightly afterward, and sunscreen is standard.
quick.risks: Stinging, redness, irritation and dryness are common, and pigment change is a reported complication. Wikipedia notes that weak home kits can cause injury and scarring.

angle.text: People use glycolic peels for brighter, smoother skin, and to fade dark marks, under-eye darkening and acne scars. The AHA loosens dead cells so skin renews faster. It is the most widely studied AHA peel, in mostly small studies.

lactic-acid-peel.summary: A mild AHA peel used for gentle brightening, dark under-eyes and melasma.

quick.overview:
A lactic acid peel is a mild alpha-hydroxy acid peel used for pigmentation such as melasma and dark under-eye skin. People choose it for a gentle route to a brighter, more even tone.

Like other AHA peels, it loosens and removes outer skin layers in a controlled way, and the skin renews. Published work is a handful of small comparative studies, mostly in Indian patients, usually comparing it with glycolic or trichloroacetic acid peels. They used it at 15% for periorbital melanosis and at 92% for epidermal melasma.
quick.how: A clinician applies it in short office sessions, typically repeated as a series. Little downtime is usual, and sunscreen is used afterward.
quick.risks: Light peels commonly cause stinging, redness, irritation and dryness. Stronger or deeper peels carry higher complication risk.

angle.text: People use lactic acid peels as a gentle way to brighten skin and soften dark under-eye circles and melasma. The mild AHA loosens dead skin so renewal speeds up and tone evens out. A few small comparisons have studied it.

mandelic-acid-peel.summary: A gentle AHA peel used for smoother, more even skin across age groups and skin tones.

quick.overview:
A mandelic acid peel is a mild alpha-hydroxy acid peel used for acne-prone, sensitive or mature skin. People choose it for smoother, more even skin with gentle exfoliation.

It is a superficial exfoliating peel, and the aesthetic literature describes it as gentle. Two small studies exist: a 2013 study on sebum secretion in mature women and a 2022 acne trial using a combined salicylic and mandelic peel. The authors of the sebum study reported no side effects.
quick.how: A clinician applies it in short sessions, often repeated as a series, with little visible downtime. It is commonly used alongside regular acne or anti-aging skincare.
quick.risks: Light peels can cause stinging, redness and dryness. Published safety data come from the two small studies.

angle.text: People use mandelic acid peels for gentle exfoliation that smooths texture and evens skin tone, including on sensitive or mature skin. The AHA loosens outer skin so it renews. Two small studies, on sebum and on acne, have examined it.

pyruvic-acid-peel.summary: A clinic-applied superficial peel using an alpha-keto acid to clear active acne and refresh congested skin.

quick.overview:
Pyruvic acid peels are superficial chemical peels applied in a clinic, mostly for acne. People book them to clear breakouts and refresh dull, congested skin.

Pyruvic acid is a keratolytic alpha-keto acid that loosens the outer skin layers so they shed, which clears pores and eases breakouts. Published work is small: a 2014 comparison of 50% pyruvic and 30% salicylic acid peels in 20 acne patients measured effects on facial sebum secretion.
quick.how: A clinician applies it in the office, and treatment is usually repeated as a series. Mild peeling follows, and sunscreen is used afterward.
quick.risks: Peels in general can cause redness, photosensitivity, pigment change and, rarely, scarring.

angle.text: People book pyruvic acid peels to clear active acne and refresh dull, congested skin. The keratolytic acid sheds the outer layer so pores clear and breakouts ease. A handful of small studies cover its use in acne.

phenol-croton-oil-peel.summary: The classic deep peel for wrinkles and skin tightening, now also done in gentler low-phenol versions.

quick.overview:
The phenol-croton oil peel is a deep chemical peel used for facial resurfacing, wrinkle reduction and skin tightening. Once healing is complete, the result is smoother, tighter skin with fewer wrinkles.

It injures the skin deeply and is followed by collagen remodeling. The classic Baker-Gordon formula from 1962 was long the standard, and reviews report that lower-phenol and lower-croton-oil formulas have largely replaced it, with a better safety profile and more natural results. Plastic surgeon Gregory Hetter argued that croton oil is the active peeling agent, with phenol acting as a carrier at lower concentrations. Evidence is mostly surgeon case series, formula studies and lab work.
quick.how: It is performed by physicians, often with sedation, followed by a recovery period of redness, crusting and peeling before the new skin settles. Aftercare includes wound care and strict sun avoidance.
quick.risks: Deep peels carry more complications: prolonged redness, pigment change including loss, atrophy and scarring. Recovery is long, and phenol has systemic effects, which is why it is physician-performed.

angle.text: People use the phenol-croton oil peel for the strongest peel-based reduction of wrinkles and skin laxity. It removes damaged skin layers, and as the skin regrows and collagen remodels the face looks smoother and firmer. It has been used since the 1962 Baker-Gordon formula, and gentler low-phenol versions are now common.

chemical-reconstruction-of-skin-scars.summary: Spot-applying strong TCA acid into individual acne scars to make them shallower.

quick.overview:
Chemical reconstruction of skin scars (CROSS) places a high-concentration TCA solution into individual depressed scars, such as ice-pick acne scars, instead of peeling the whole face. People use it to make specific scars shallower and the skin surface smoother.

The acid is said to trigger a focal wound-healing response in the base of the scar, so new collagen gradually fills it. Published work in the sources reviewed is limited to small registered trials.
quick.how: A clinician dabs the acid into each scar, and the treated spots crust and heal over days. It is often repeated in sessions a few weeks apart, with visible improvement building over repeated rounds.
quick.risks: TCA can cause redness, pigment change and scarring. It is performed by clinicians.

angle.text: People with ice-pick and other atrophic acne scars use CROSS to make individual scars shallower without treating the whole face. Strong TCA in the scar base prompts new collagen, so the scar floor rebuilds. Small trials have studied it for this use.

skinvive.summary: Microdroplet hyaluronic acid injected into the skin for a hydrated glow and smoother texture, without added volume.

quick.overview:
Skinvive (Juvederm Volite) is an Allergan hyaluronic acid injectable placed in many tiny droplets within the skin itself. People choose it for a hydrated, glassy glow and finer texture rather than added volume.

Hyaluronic acid binds water, so skin can look plumper, more hydrated and smoother. Published evidence is small and recent, including a 2025 split-face trial of combined botulinum toxin and Skinvive and several manufacturer-linked registered trials, one of them on neck lines.
quick.how: A clinician injects it across the cheeks or other areas in a single session of microdroplets. People often repeat it a few times a year and combine it with other skin treatments or neurotoxin.
quick.risks: Filler injections can cause redness, swelling and bruising, and less commonly granulomas. It is clinician-administered.

angle.text: Skinvive is used for a hydrated, glassy glow and smoother texture rather than added volume. Hyaluronic acid placed in microdroplets within the skin binds water, so skin looks plumper and finer-textured. Evidence so far is early, from recent small trials.

profhilo-structura.summary: A hybrid hyaluronic acid injectable used to restore cheek volume and contour for a fuller, lifted midface.

quick.overview:
Profhilo Structura is a hybrid hyaluronic acid product from IBSA, injected into superficial facial fat layers, mainly the lateral cheek. People use it for a fuller, lifted, better-supported midface.

It combines high- and low-molecular-weight hyaluronic acid into stable complexes using the NAHYCO process, without chemical cross-linking, and is described as addressing the loss of facial fat volume with age rather than acting as a conventional bolus filler. Authors propose it may influence fat tissue homeostasis, which is a hypothesis. Published data are a 22-person case series, an observational pilot study and lab comparisons, with a 164-person trial registered as ongoing.
quick.how: A clinician injects it with a cannula into each side of the face. Treatment is typically a short course of sessions, and results are described as developing over the following weeks.
quick.risks: Risks described for injectable hyaluronic acid include bruising, swelling and injection-site reactions. Product-specific safety data come from small studies, and it is given by trained clinicians.

angle.text: People use Profhilo Structura to restore cheek volume and lift the midface. The hybrid hyaluronic acid is placed in superficial fat compartments to rebuild contour in the lateral cheek. Evidence so far is small case series.

profhilo-body.summary: A hybrid hyaluronic acid skin booster used for firmer, smoother skin on the arms and hands.

quick.overview:
Profhilo Body is an IBSA hybrid hyaluronic acid injectable used by clinicians to treat laxity and roughness of body skin, such as the upper inner arms and backs of the hands. People use it for smoother, firmer-looking skin there.

It uses hybrid complexes of high- and low-molecular-weight hyaluronic acid injected into the skin to improve skin quality rather than add bulk. Published evidence includes a 12-month single-arm study of women with upper-arm laxity, a completed trial on the backs of the hands and a post-marketing safety review. These are small and mostly uncontrolled.
quick.how: A clinician injects it into the skin of the area in a short course of sessions. Results are described as building over the following weeks.
quick.risks: A post-marketing review has assessed adverse event reports across the product family. Injections carry general risks such as bruising and swelling, and it is given by trained clinicians.

angle.text: People use Profhilo Body to firm and smooth lax or rough skin on the upper arms and backs of the hands. Hybrid hyaluronic acid injected into the skin hydrates and tightens it. Small single-arm trials have studied it.

rejuran-hb.summary: A polynucleotide skin-booster injectable used in clinics for smoother, better-quality skin.

quick.overview:
Rejuran HB is a polynucleotide injectable used in aesthetic clinics as a skin booster. People use it for smoother, healthier-looking skin texture and quality.

Polynucleotides are chains of nucleotides, and skin booster products inject them into the skin, where they are generally described as supporting repair and hydration. Rejuran products are referred to in the literature as a family that includes Rejuran S and Rejuran HB Plus. The only published study identified is a rabbit experiment on accidental arterial injection, and no human trials of Rejuran HB were found.
quick.how: A clinician injects it into the skin, typically as a short series of sessions. People use it as a skin-quality treatment rather than for volume.
quick.risks: The rabbit study examined vascular behavior of polynucleotide products after accidental intra-arterial exposure. Human safety data were not found in the sources reviewed.

angle.text: People use Rejuran HB as a skin booster for smoother, more even skin quality. Injected polynucleotides are described as supporting skin repair and hydration. Published human data for this product are very limited.

juvelook.summary: A Korean PDLLA-hyaluronic acid biostimulator injected for tear troughs, folds and skin texture.

quick.overview:
Juvelook is a poly-D,L-lactic acid (PDLLA) injectable from VAIM Inc. of Seoul, used by clinicians as a skin booster and collagen stimulator under the eyes, in nasolabial folds, forehead, cheeks, clavicle and pores. People use it for smoother tear troughs, softer folds and better skin texture.

PDLLA is described as a biostimulator that prompts the body to produce collagen over time, so skin thickens and firms. Published reports describe a PDLLA and hyaluronic acid hybrid, with variants named Juvelook Volume and Juvelook GLAM. The literature is mainly small studies, case series and case reports, plus animal research.
quick.how: A clinician injects it, usually in a short series of sessions, with improvement building gradually as collagen forms.
quick.risks: Reported problems include firm nodules after tear trough injection, and a rabbit study examined accidental intra-arterial injection. It is performed by trained clinicians.

angle.text: People use Juvelook to smooth tear troughs and folds and improve skin texture. The PDLLA stimulates collagen so skin thickens and firms over time. Support comes from small studies and case reports.

lenisna.summary: A PDLLA injectable booster used in aesthetic clinics to firm and smooth skin through collagen stimulation.

quick.overview:
Lenisna is a poly-D,L-lactic acid (PDLLA) injectable used in aesthetic clinics as a skin booster and collagen stimulator. People use PDLLA products for firmer, smoother skin.

PDLLA-HA products combine PDLLA microspheres, which stimulate collagen, with non-cross-linked hyaluronic acid as a carrier. The only source found is a 2026 expert consensus on safe injection technique for PDLLA-HA200, and efficacy studies of Lenisna were not found.
quick.how: A clinician injects it, and collagen-driven changes are described as building gradually after treatment.
quick.risks: The consensus describes a rare but serious complication: visual field impairment and blindness after accidental injection into a blood vessel, and sets out management recommendations. It is performed by trained clinicians.

angle.text: People use Lenisna as a skin booster for firmer, smoother skin. PDLLA microspheres are meant to stimulate collagen production. The main literature is a 2026 consensus on injection safety, and efficacy studies were not found.

aesthefill.summary: A Korean PDLLA microsphere biostimulator that firms skin and softens lines gradually by stimulating collagen.

quick.overview:
AestheFill is a PDLLA microsphere injectable from REGEN Biotech of Seoul, used by clinicians to restore facial volume and, increasingly, body contour. People use it for firmer skin and softer lines that develop gradually.

It contains PDLLA microspheres with carboxymethyl cellulose as a suspending agent, is described as biodegradable and biostimulatory, and prompts tissue to rebuild collagen and volume over time. A randomized, evaluator-blinded multicentre study compared it with hyaluronic acid for nasolabial folds, and much of the other literature concerns reconstitution methods and consensus technique recommendations.
quick.how: It is supplied as a powder that the clinician reconstitutes with sterile water before injection. Treatment is usually a short series of sessions, with results building over weeks to months.
quick.risks: Technique-related issues such as lumping during reconstitution are discussed in the literature, and specific adverse event rates were not summarised in the sources reviewed. It is administered by trained clinicians.

angle.text: People use AestheFill to firm skin and soften lines like nasolabial folds gradually. The PDLLA microspheres stimulate collagen so tissue rebuilds over time. A randomized trial compared it with hyaluronic acid for nasolabial folds.
